source_text: CAPUT TRICESIMUM SEXTUM, De primo hominis statu. STant status, per quos ad summam perfectionem, ad quam conditus est, perducitur. II. Estque primus aut primum secutus. Quatuor status hominis communiter distinguuntur a Theologis: creationis, lapsionis, regenerationis et beatitudinis, seu confectionis, defectionis, refectionis et perfectionis, seu innocentiae, peccati, gratiae et gloriae. III. Primus est, in quo homo a Deo creatore conditus ac lege peculiari circumscriptus est. Legis formula homini in hoc statu praescripta exstat Gen. 2:16-17, ac repetitur Siracid. 15:14-18. Quam Adamus facile praestare potuit et nulla necessitate compulsus violavit. Si enim necessario violasset, ea necessitas fuisset aut a natura aut a Diabolo aut a Deo. A natura non fuit, quia homo conditus est liberi arbitrii, neque aliter si esset, id dissimulasset Adamus cum de accusatione sui laboraret (Gen. 3:12). Neque a diabolo fuit, quia suadere potuit, cogere non potuit. Neque enim diabolus hominem decepisset, nisi iam ille sibi placere coepisset, ut ait Augustinus (de Civ. Dei XIV.13). Neque a Deo, quia fecit eum bonum et ad imaginem sui (Gen. 1:27; 5:1).
english: CHAPTER THIRTY-SIX. On the first state of the human being.

There stand the states through which the human being is led to the highest perfection for which he was made. II. And it is either the first or that which followed the first. Theologians commonly distinguish four states of the human: of creation, of falling, of regeneration, and of blessedness — or of constitution, defection, restoration, and perfection — or of innocence, sin, grace, and glory.

III. The first is that in which the human was made by God the creator and circumscribed by a peculiar law. The formula of the law prescribed to the human in this state stands in Genesis 2:16-17 and is repeated in Sirach 15:14-18. Adam could easily keep it and violated it compelled by no necessity. For if he had necessarily violated it, that necessity would have been from nature, or from the Devil, or from God. It was not from nature, because the human was made of free choice; nor, if it were otherwise, would Adam have concealed it when laboring under accusation of himself (Genesis 3:12). Nor was it from the devil, because he could persuade, not compel. For the devil would not have deceived the human unless he had already begun to please himself, as Augustine says (City of God XIV.13). Nor from God, because He made him good and after His own image (Genesis 1:27; 5:1).

source_text: IV. Estque hic status partim animalis, partim spiritualis. Ut enim rectius intelligamus ea quae de imagine Dei dicta sunt, eoque pleniorem ac distinctiorem subiecti nostri cognitionem habeamus, particulatim consideranda veniunt tum quae naturalia tum quae supernaturalia in homine recens creato occurrunt, sive quid et quantum in statu purorum naturalium potuerit; unde postmodum facile elicitur quid nunc amissis supernaturalibus in statu peccati possit. V. Animalis est, quatenus homo e naturali corporis et animae unione anima corpori suo bona procurat, et corpore vicissim animae ad officia naturae ac desideria ipsius convenientia praesto est. Haec pars primi status, in quo homo conditus est, fundatur naturali animae et corporis unione et vita, quam anima naturaliter vivit in corpore. Ex qua unione et vita est, quod anima corpori bona sua procurat, et corpus animae praesto est ad officia naturae ipsius congruentia. Et secundum hunc statum est inter hominem et bona huius mundi mutuus respectus, qui efficit ut homo ea desiderare, et iis sibi acquirendis operam quam sibi necessariam et congruentem iudicat collocare possit. Quae pars primi status, si sola et sine ordine ad spiritualia seu supernaturalia consideretur, purorum naturalium a scholis dicitur.
english: IV. And this state is partly animal, partly spiritual. For that we may more rightly understand what has been said of the image of God, and so have a fuller and more distinct knowledge of our subject, we must consider in detail both what is natural and what is supernatural in the newly created human — or what and how much he could do in the state of pure naturals; whence afterward it is easily drawn out what, the supernatural gifts now lost, he can do in the state of sin.

V. It is animal insofar as, from the natural union of body and soul, the soul procures goods for its body, and by the body in turn the soul is ready for the offices of nature and for desires fitting to it. This part of the first state in which the human was made is founded on the natural union of soul and body and on the life the soul naturally lives in the body. From that union and life it is that the soul procures its goods for the body, and the body is ready for the soul unto offices congruent with its nature. And according to this state there is a mutual respect between the human and the goods of this world, which makes it that the human can desire them and put forth the effort he judges necessary and fitting for acquiring them. Which part of the first state, if considered alone and without order to spiritual or supernatural things, is called by the schools the state of pure naturals.

source_text: VI. Spiritualis est, quatenus homo ex speciali Dei gratia et favore in intellectu luce divina, in voluntate rectitudine et sanctitate, in affectibus harmonia et ordine praeditus erat, adeo ut Deum cognosceret, amaret, et ei obediret ex toto corde, et proximos tanquam se ipsum. In hoc statu imago Dei primigenia consistebat, non in sola animae immortalitate aut rationis usu, sed in vera iustitia et sanctitate (Eph. 4:24; Col. 3:10), qua homo Deo placebat et ei inserviebat. Habebat intellectum lucidum sine culpabili ignorantia, voluntatem rectam sine prava inclinatione ad malum, et affectus ordinatos sine perturbatione. Potuit non peccare, non tamen non potuit peccare — hoc est, libertas ad utrumque, non necessitas ad bonum solum. Arbor vitae et arbor scientiae boni et mali in paradiso signa erant huius status et probationis.
english: VI. It is spiritual insofar as the human, from Gods special grace and favor, was endowed in the intellect with divine light, in the will with uprightness and holiness, and in the affections with harmony and order, so that he knew God, loved Him, and obeyed Him from the whole heart, and neighbors as himself. In this state the first image of God consisted, not in the mere immortality of the soul or use of reason, but in true righteousness and holiness (Ephesians 4:24; Colossians 3:10), by which the human pleased God and served Him. He had a lucid intellect without culpable ignorance, an upright will without a crooked inclination to evil, and ordered affections without disturbance. He was able not to sin, yet he was not unable to sin — that is, liberty toward both, not necessity toward the good alone. The tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in paradise were signs of this state and of its probation.

source_text: VII. Sunt autem de hoc primo hominis statu notandae observationes. 1. Homo in primo statu creatus est integer et integer mansisset, nisi libera voluntate peccasset. 2. Dominium in creaturas inferiores ei datum est (Gen. 1:28), non tyrannicum sed paternum et oeconomicum. 3. Labor in paradiso non erat poena sed delectatio et exercitium. 4. Mors non erat naturalis necessitati subiecta in hoc statu, sed poena peccati denunciata. 5. Societas coniugalis instituta est ante lapsum in sanctitate et amore mutuo. 6. Primus parens imaginem Dei primigenii status felicem integritatem, tanquam author humani generis, a Deo acceperat, ut ita per eam totus Deo placeret et inserviret. Haec observatio patet e dictis. Nulla hic macula erat, sed summa puritas; nulla culpabilis ignorantia, sed egregia scientia; nulla a Deo aversio, sed amor integer.
english: VII. Observations are to be noted concerning this first state of the human. First, the human in the first state was created whole and would have remained whole had he not sinned by free will. Second, dominion over inferior creatures was given him (Genesis 1:28), not tyrannical but paternal and household-like. Third, labor in paradise was not a punishment but a delight and exercise. Fourth, death was not subject to natural necessity in this state, but was the punishment of sin as denounced. Fifth, conjugal society was instituted before the fall in holiness and mutual love.

Sixth, the first parent had received from God the happy integrity of the image of God of the first state, as author of the human race, so that through it he might wholly please God and serve Him. This observation is plain from what has been said. Here there was no stain, but highest purity; no culpable ignorance, but outstanding knowledge; no aversion from God, but whole love.

source_text: In primo etiam statu unus fuisset ordo politicus sine divisione imperiorum per peccatum introducta. Primus et unus dominus orbis terrarum fuit Adam, secundus Seth, tertius qui optimus ex descendentibus — et propterea divisum est imperium, quia peccaverunt homines, ac diviserunt agros et dominia et regnum usurparunt. Et introductum est ius gentium per iniquitatem, ut docet S. Clemens, quod retinetur ex permissione, non ex imperio Dei, qui omnes vivere in communi voluit, ut idem testatur, et Ambrosius, et Chrysostomus et meliores patres. Unde et Salomon ait: propter peccata terrae, multi principes eius. In principio enim fuisset idem rex et pater et summus sacerdos reipublicae et supremus in toto mundo a Deo dependens, ut Melchisedechus. Proptereaque Christus omnes principes sub sui unius pastoris imperium revocavit, cum ad saeculum illud restituendum venit (Ezech. 34:23; Ioh. 10:16). Nec bella, fames, haereses, schismata, pestes cessabunt, donec omnes principes terrae sub unius potestatem redacti unum senatum habeant, vivantque concordes. Id quod fiet plane, ubi ex hac militia et peregrinatione transibimus in patriam aeternae quietis et triumphi. Frustra enim sunt Chiliastae, qui hoc sperant in terra huius militiae, et pontificii, qui violenter affectant.
english: In the first state also there would have been one political order without the division of empires introduced by sin. The first and sole lord of the circle of the earth was Adam, the second Seth, the third whoever was best among the descendants — and therefore empire was divided, because humans sinned, and divided fields and dominions, and usurped kingship. And the law of nations was introduced through iniquity, as holy Clement teaches, which is retained by permission, not by Gods command, who willed all to live in common, as the same witnesses, and Ambrose, and Chrysostom, and the better fathers. Hence also Solomon says: because of the sins of the land, many are its princes.

For in the beginning the same one would have been king and father and highest priest of the commonwealth and supreme in the whole world, depending on God, as Melchizedek. And therefore Christ recalled all princes under the empire of Himself as one shepherd, when He came to restore that age (Ezekiel 34:23; John 10:16). Nor will wars, famine, heresies, schisms, and plagues cease until all the princes of the earth, brought under one power, have one senate and live in concord. Which will plainly happen when from this warfare and pilgrimage we pass into the homeland of eternal rest and triumph. For the Chiliasts are vain who hope this on the earth of this warfare, and the papal party who violently grasp at it.
